assessment.nobel_worthiness: Founded modern political economics, with a unified formal and empirical treatment of how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and public-goods provision. The work is foundational, widely taught, and has spawned a large empirical literature. It is conceptually distinct from the recent institutions-and-growth prize.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central pair, with decades of joint work including the integrative books on political economics. Besley is a close third through state capacity, accountability and the citizen-candidate tradition. Others, such as Alesina and Acemoglu, are not on this ballot or already honoured.
assessment.maturity: Contributions date from the 1990s and have long been confirmed by replication, extension and policy use. The timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Possible overlap in the committee's mind with the 2024 prize on institutions.
Whether the third credit should go to Besley or to a scholar outside the listed names.
Some empirical results on electoral-rule effects are debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Created the law-and-finance field by showing that legal origins and investor protection systematically relate to financial development and corporate ownership. It is among the most cited bodies of work in economics and has changed research and policy on corporate governance.
assessment.attribution: The LLSV collaboration is a clear core trio, with Vishny as the fourth credited name. The three-laureate limit forces a difficult choice, and Shleifer's broader contributions would also support a separate credit.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from 1997–2008 and have had ample time for scrutiny and for follow-up work.
uncertainties: The legal-origins thesis has been challenged on measurement, causality and endogeneity.
The Vishny/Shleifer attribution question.
Controversy surrounding some individuals' careers may affect consensus.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firms framework reshaped trade theory and empirics. It explains selection, exporter premia and welfare gains from trade beyond the representative-firm model. It is a clear conceptual advance with deep empirical validation.
assessment.attribution: Melitz's 2003 model is the pivotal contribution. Helpman has major prior and parallel work on firm heterogeneity and on trade theory more broadly. Redding is an important contributor to quantitative extensions, but the two-name credit is the cleanest.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation in a very large literature, with firm-level data now standard.
uncertainties: Overlap with the neighbouring quantitative-trade and Helpman–Grossman candidates.
Whether the committee prefers to credit Melitz alone or add Bernard/Eaton/Kortum, who are outside this ballot.
Trade has had one prize (2008), and its recency affects the field balance but not the merit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Made empirical industrial organisation practical through random-coefficients demand estimation (BLP), dynamic industry models and productivity estimation. These methods are used widely in antitrust, merger analysis and regulation. The impact on applied microeconomics is high.
assessment.attribution: Pakes is the central intellectual figure across demand, dynamics and production-function estimation. The BLP trio is natural for the demand-estimation credit. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are significant but would stretch the three-laureate limit.
assessment.maturity: BLP dates from 1995, and the methodology is firmly established and still extended.
uncertainties: Whether the committee credits method or the underlying IO discoveries.
How to split credit among a large group.
Little prior recognition of structural IO as a prize area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework and its monetary-policy rules underpin the way central banks think and model. The contributions combine theory, estimation and practical policy influence, and the work is deeply embedded in institutional practice.
assessment.attribution: Highly diffuse across Calvo (pricing), Taylor (rules), Woodford and Gali (canonical framework), and Christiano–Eichenbaum (estimated models). Any three-name selection leaves out major contributors, so credit assignment is the principal difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature after more than 25 years of use, though parts of the framework were challenged after the financial crisis and the pandemic.
uncertainties: Attribution is highly contested.
The 2022 macro-banking award and the macro-finance debates may affect the field's relative position.
The framework's adequacy for inflation dynamics after 2021 is debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Documented the labour-market effects of import competition and of automation, and advanced the task-based view of technology. This is influential in both academic and policy debate and rests on credible research designs.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock papers by Autor, Dorn and Hanson are a coherent unit. Katz's long-standing work on skill demand is also significant. Task-model foundations also involve scholars outside the list, which complicates the credit.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 2010s and its effects on political economy are well documented, but the long-run interpretation is still being debated.
uncertainties: Replications and critiques on magnitudes and persistence.
Relative recency compared with other candidates.
Overlap with the 2025 prize on technology-driven growth and with Goldin's 2023 prize on labour markets.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model is a cornerstone of non-cooperative game theory and a building block for models in labour, trade, macroeconomics and market design. The conceptual and technical contribution is first-rate.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein's 1982 paper is the central result, and the Rubinstein–Wolinsky market-bargaining model extended it. Binmore's contributions on the bargaining foundations are real but secondary. Stahl and Ståhl-related work is outside the list.
assessment.maturity: More than forty years of use. This is a long-delayed, fully mature contribution.
uncertainties: Possible reluctance to reward another game-theory topic soon after the 2020 prize on auctions and the 2007 and 2012 prizes on mechanisms and matching.
Whether the committee views the model as a single result rather than a body of work.
Candidate age and the question of Rubinstein's public statements.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Constructed long-run historical series on top incomes and wealth, changing the empirical basis of distributional debates and tax-policy research. The impact on research agendas and public discussion is very large.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the originators of the top-income-share series, and Zucman is a distinct, younger contributor on offshore wealth and wealth taxation. Atkinson's earlier role is relevant but he is deceased.
assessment.maturity: The top-income series date from the early 2000s and are widely used, but the wealth-concentration and tax-evasion estimates are newer and contested.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over wealth-inequality measurement.
The extent to which the contribution is data construction rather than theory or identification.
Policy-advocacy concerns may affect committee consensus.
Saez also appears on other ballots, so attribution overlaps.
